<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and README, this project is the compiler for Teal—a typed dialect of Lua. The repository is structured as a compiler project that includes both the core compiler engine (implemented in tl.lua and tl.tl) and extensive language specifications, tests (under spec/...), documentation (docs/…), and CI/CD configuration. Here’s how you can design an accurate system architecture diagram:

1. Main Project Components:
   • Compiler Engine: This is the heart of the project and is primarily contained in the single-file core (tl.lua) and its Teal counterpart (tl.tl). It encapsulates the logic that reads, parses, type-checks, and compiles Teal code.
   • Command-line Interface (CLI): Teal supports subcommands (such as run, check, gen, warnings) that enable users to invoke the compiler in different modes. This layer also deals with reading command-line arguments, configuration files (tlconfig.lua), and applying compiler options.
   • Loader and Integration Module: The compiler supports on-the-fly Teal file compilation with the package loader (via tl.loader()). Represent this as a dedicated component that integrates with Lua’s require() mechanism.
   • Build Tool Integration: Although not part of the core code, the README suggests integration with Cyan (a separate build tool designed for Teal). This external dependency layer can be noted as an optional tool that interacts with the compiler.
   • Testing & Specification Framework: With a rich “spec” directory subdivided into various subdirectories (api, cli, lang, etc.), this part of the project ensures that each language component (lexer, parser, code generation, inference, subtyping, etc.) is thoroughly tested. It documents expected behavior for all compiler phases.
   • Documentation and Community Support Components: The docs/ directory (including tutorial, compiler options, macroexp, grammar, etc.) and other files (CHANGELOG, LICENSE, etc.) provide guidelines for users and contributors but are less central to the runtime architecture. They might be included as peripheral supporting components in your diagram.

2. Detail of the Compiler Engine (Core Pipeline):
   • Input: Teal source files (.tl) provided by the user.
   • Lexical Analysis: Represent the lexer component (see spec/lang/lexer and related tests). It breaks down the input source code into tokens.
   • Parsing: Show the parser module (spec/lang/parser) that converts tokens into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
   • Type Analysis & Inference: Diagram a module that handles type checking, inference, and subtyping. This links to parts of the spec that cover declarations, assignments, inference, and subtyping.
   • Macro Expansion & Code Generation: Include components for macro expansion (spec/lang/macroexp) and code generation (spec/lang/code_gen), where the compiler converts the typed AST into plain Lua code (removing type annotations).
   • Error Reporting: There is a dedicated element for error reporting (spec/lang/error_reporting), ensuring that syntax and type errors are well-captured.

3. Communication / Data Flow Among Components:
   • Show directional arrows that display the sequential data flow: starting from the CLI input → loader or file input → lexer → parser → type analysis/inference → code generation → output (either immediate execution in “run” mode or generation of a Lua file in “gen” mode).
   • Additionally, show arrows from configuration files (tlconfig.lua, docs/compiler_options.md) feeding into the CLI control flow.
   • For the testing modules in the “spec” directory, indicate that these validate interactions between each of the components.

4. Architectural and Design Patterns:
   • The design is modular. Even though the core compiler begins as a single file, the extensive spec directory reflects a clear separation of concerns (e.g., separate modules for lexer, parser, and type system).
   • The compiler’s integration as a loader for Lua represents an adapter-like pattern that plugs into Lua’s require mechanism.
   • The use of subcommands in the CLI suggests a Command pattern for handling different user inputs.
   • The testing framework is organized to mirror the compiler internals, indicating a design that values high-testability and modularity.

5. Diagramming Guidelines:
   • Clearly label each component (CLI, Loader/Integration, Lexer, Parser, Type Checker, Code Generator, Error Reporter, and Testing Modules) with descriptive names.
   • Use directional arrows to show the flow from input (source files & configuration) through the compilation stages to output (execution or generated .lua file).
   • Consider using different colors or shapes to differentiate core runtime modules (like the compiler pipeline) from peripheral components (like docs, community, and tests).
   • Optionally, include a legend that associates file paths or spec directories with corresponding architectural components.
   • Emphasize in your diagram how external integrations (Cyan for building projects, editor plugins for Teal, etc.) connect to the core compiler engine.

6. Tailoring the Diagram to This Project:
   • Since this is a compiler for a programming language, focus on the compilation pipeline (lexical analysis, parsing, type-checking, macro expansion, code generation) along with the CLI that triggers these processes.
   • Include an optional branch showing the integration with the Lua package loader (via tl.loader()), which highlights how Teal files are processed on-demand.
   • Also, include a section on testing that shows how the multiple “spec” submodules feed back into ensuring the reliability of each stage of the compiler.

Following this outline will help you construct a detailed, accurate, and project-tailored system design diagram that captures the essential architectural elements of the Teal compiler. Make sure that in your final diagram, each component is clearly marked and connected with directional arrows that explain data flow, thereby providing a comprehensive overview of how the Teal compiler processes code from input to output.
</explanation>
